subQuestions.questionText: Why would a decrease in South African exports lead to the depreciation of the rand?
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: A decrease in exports reduces the demand for the rand by foreigners (who would otherwise buy rands to pay for South African goods). The reduced demand for the rand causes its value to fall (depreciate) against other currencies.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term progressive tax.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: A progressive tax is a tax where the tax rate increases as the taxable income increases. Higher-income earners pay a larger proportion of their income as tax than lower-income earners (e.g. personal income tax in South Africa).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the effect of a regressive tax system on income distribution.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: A regressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from low-income earners than from high-income earners. This worsens income inequality and widens the gap between the rich and the poor.

subQuestions.questionText: Why will tax revenue decrease if the government imposes very high tax rates?
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer (2 x 2 marks): (1) Very high tax rates discourage work effort and productivity, which reduces taxable income. (2) High tax rates encourage tax evasion and avoidance, leading to less tax actually collected. (3) High taxes may push businesses and skilled workers to emigrate or relocate, shrinking the tax base.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term recession.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: A recession is a period of declining economic activity, typically defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP. It is characterised by falling output, rising unemployment and reduced consumer spending.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the impact of the Ukraine/Russia war on local food prices.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of wheat, sunflower oil and fertilisers. The war has disrupted global supply chains, reducing supply and pushing up world prices, which feed through to higher local food prices in South Africa (imported inflation).

subQuestions.questionText: How can the government use monetary policy to stimulate economic activity?
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer (2 x 2 marks): (1) The South African Reserve Bank can lower the repo rate, making borrowing cheaper for consumers and businesses, which encourages spending and investment. (2) The SARB can buy government securities in the open market, increasing the money supply and stimulating economic activity. (3) The SARB can lower the cash reserve requirement so commercial banks have more money available to extend credit. (4) Moral suasion can be used to encourage banks to extend credit during a downturn.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss the free-floating and the fixed exchange rate systems. (2 x 4)
subQuestions.topic: Foreign Exchange â€” Exchange Rate Systems
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (4 marks each):

Free-floating exchange rate system:
- The exchange rate is determined entirely by the market forces of demand and supply for the currency.
- There is no government or central bank intervention.
- Rates fluctuate continuously in response to trade flows, capital flows and market expectations.
- Advantage: automatic adjustment of the balance of payments. Disadvantage: high volatility creates uncertainty.

Fixed exchange rate system:
- The government or central bank fixes (pegs) the exchange rate at a chosen level against another currency or basket of currencies.
- The central bank intervenes by buying or selling foreign currency to maintain the peg.
- It must hold large reserves of foreign currency to defend the rate.
- Advantage: stability and certainty for trade and investment. Disadvantage: loss of independent monetary policy and pressure on reserves.

subQuestions.questionText: How can the South African government improve the quality of public sector provisioning? (4 x 2)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (4 x 2 marks):
- Improve accountability through performance audits and consequence management for poor service delivery.
- Reduce corruption and wasteful expenditure by strengthening oversight bodies (Auditor-General, Public Protector).
- Invest in skills training and capacity-building for public sector employees.
- Use efficient costing methods (zero-base budgeting, performance budgeting) to ensure value for money.
- Privatise or partner with the private sector (PPPs) where appropriate to bring in expertise and efficiency.
- Implement Batho Pele principles to focus on citizen-centred service delivery.
- Strengthen monitoring and evaluation systems to track outcomes.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term protectionism.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: Protectionism is a trade policy in which a government uses tariffs, quotas, subsidies and other measures to restrict imports and protect domestic industries from foreign competition.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain a disadvantage when applying the protectionism policy.
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer: Protectionism leads to higher prices for consumers because cheaper imports are restricted. It can also reduce competition, which causes domestic producers to become inefficient and may invite retaliatory trade barriers from other countries.

subQuestions.questionText: How can the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) negatively affect South Africa?
subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer (2 x 2 marks): (1) South Africa may become over-dependent on the US market, leaving it vulnerable if AGOA is not renewed beyond 2025. (2) Local industries face increased competition from US goods entering South Africa, which can damage domestic producers. (3) AGOA's eligibility conditions may force policy decisions that compromise South African sovereignty. (4) Benefits are unevenly distributed across sectors, mainly favouring exporters of automotive and agricultural goods.

subQuestions.memoText: Memo not provided. Expected answer (2 x 2 marks): (1) Invest in education and skills training to improve productivity and employability. (2) Improve access to healthcare through the National Health Insurance and clinics. (3) Provide social grants to vulnerable households to alleviate poverty. (4) Invest in infrastructure (housing, water, electricity, sanitation) to improve quality of life. (5) Create jobs through public works programmes and supporting small businesses.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss partnerships and good governance as benchmark criteria for regional development. (2 x 4)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (4 marks each):

Partnerships:
- Effective regional development requires partnerships between government, business, communities and civil society.
- Public-private partnerships pool financial and technical resources for large infrastructure projects.
- International partnerships (e.g. with development banks, donor countries) bring funding and expertise.
- Cross-border partnerships in regions such as SADC promote integrated development.

Good governance:
- Transparent, accountable and corruption-free administration is essential to attract investment.
- Sound institutions (rule of law, property rights, independent judiciary) build investor confidence.
- Effective service delivery at local government level supports development outcomes.
- Citizen participation in decision-making improves legitimacy and policy quality.

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate the impact of export promotion on local industries in South Africa. (4 x 2)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (4 x 2 marks):

Positive impacts:
- Larger markets allow local industries to achieve economies of scale, reducing average costs.
- Exporting increases foreign exchange earnings and supports the balance of payments.
- Exposure to international competition forces local producers to improve quality and efficiency.
- Job creation in export-oriented industries reduces unemployment.

Negative impacts:
- Local industries may become over-dependent on volatile foreign markets.
- Subsidies and incentives for exporters can be costly to government and may distort resource allocation.
- Domestic prices may rise as producers prioritise export markets.
- Vulnerability to exchange rate fluctuations can hurt profitability.

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a well-labelled Phillips curve, explain the relationship between inflation and unemployment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (8 marks):

Graph requirements (max 4 marks):
- Correct labelling of the axes: y-axis = Inflation rate (%), x-axis = Unemployment rate (%) â€” 1 mark
- Correct labelling on the axes (numerical values) â€” 1 mark
- Correct downward-sloping Phillips Curve drawn â€” 1 mark
- Indication of trade-off points on the curve â€” 1 mark

Explanation (max 4 marks):
- The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment.
- When unemployment is low, demand for labour is high, pushing wages up, which leads to higher inflation.
- When unemployment is high, there is downward pressure on wages, reducing inflationary pressure.
- Policymakers face a short-run trade-off: reducing unemployment requires accepting higher inflation, and vice versa.
- In the long run, this trade-off may break down (stagflation), with both inflation and unemployment rising together.

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the demand-side and supply-side factors that influence economic growth in South Africa. (4 x 2)
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Expected answer (4 x 2 marks):

Demand-side factors:
- Household consumption expenditure: higher consumer spending boosts aggregate demand and stimulates production.
- Investment spending: increased private and public investment in capital goods raises productive capacity.
- Government spending: expansionary fiscal policy on infrastructure and services raises aggregate demand.
- Net exports: stronger exports relative to imports add to aggregate demand and growth.

Supply-side factors:
- Labour: a skilled, productive workforce raises potential output.
- Capital: more and better-quality capital (machinery, infrastructure) lifts productive capacity.
- Natural resources: abundance and efficient use of resources support growth.
- Technology and innovation: technological progress raises productivity.
- Entrepreneurship: more entrepreneurs lead to new businesses and jobs.

questions.title: QUESTION 5: MACROECONOMICS (Essay â€” Section C, choose one of Q5 or Q6)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail the markets within the four-sector circular flow model. (26 marks) How can the increase in injections impact on the South African economy? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Essay rubric (from question paper):

INTRODUCTION (Max 2 marks):
- Lower-order response describing the main concept (e.g. defining the four-sector circular flow model: households, firms, government, foreign sector).
- Do NOT include any part of the question.
- Do NOT repeat the introduction in the body.

BODY â€” MAIN PART (Max 26 marks): Discuss in detail the markets within the four-sector circular flow model:
- Goods market (product market): where households buy goods and services from firms; flow of goods/services and consumption expenditure.
- Factor market (resource market): where households sell factors of production (labour, land, capital, entrepreneurship) to firms in return for income (wages, rent, interest, profit).
- Financial market: where savings flow from households/firms to investors via banks and financial institutions; covers savings and investment leakages and injections.
- Foreign sector market: where the country exchanges goods, services and capital with the rest of the world (imports/exports).
- Government participation: government taxes, spends, and transfers across all markets.
(Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings/examples.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10 marks): How can an increase in injections impact on the South African economy?
- Investment (I): higher investment increases productive capacity, employment and growth.
- Government spending (G): boosts aggregate demand, supports infrastructure, creates jobs.
- Exports (X): increased export earnings improve the BoP, generate foreign exchange and create export-related jobs.
- Multiplier effect: injections lead to a multiplied increase in national income.
- Possible negative impacts: inflation if supply cannot match demand; pressure on imports.
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2 marks): Higher-order conclusion with a summary, opinion, recommendation or contradictory viewpoint with motivation.

TOTAL: 40 marks.

questions.title: QUESTION 6: ECONOMIC PURSUITS (Essay â€” Section C, choose one of Q5 or Q6)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss in detail the various social indicators. (26 marks) How can urbanisation influence the standard of living of the South African population? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.topic: Economic Pursuits â€” Social Indicators and Urbanisation
subQuestions.memoText:
Memo not provided. Essay rubric (from question paper):

INTRODUCTION (Max 2 marks):
- Lower-order response describing the main concept (e.g. defining social indicators as statistics that measure the well-being and quality of life of a population).

BODY â€” MAIN PART (Max 26 marks): Discuss in detail the various social indicators:
- Demographics: population size, growth rate, age structure, urbanisation rate.
- Health: life expectancy at birth; infant mortality rate; maternal mortality; access to healthcare; HIV/AIDS prevalence.
- Education: literacy rate; mean and expected years of schooling; school enrolment ratios; quality of education.
- Services: access to clean water, sanitation, electricity, housing.
- Nutrition: food security; calorie intake; rates of malnutrition.
- Income distribution: Gini coefficient; poverty headcount.
- Employment: unemployment rate; labour force participation.
(Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for headings/examples.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10 marks): How can urbanisation influence the standard of living?
- Positive: better access to jobs, education, healthcare and services in cities; higher incomes; broader cultural and economic opportunities.
- Negative: overcrowding, informal settlements, pressure on infrastructure and housing; rising urban unemployment; environmental pollution; increased crime.
- Net effect depends on government planning and ability to provide infrastructure and services to absorb urban growth.
(Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2 marks): Higher-order conclusion with a summary, opinion, recommendation or contradictory viewpoint with motivation.

TOTAL: 40 marks.
